title: Trust Falls, Trust Fails, and the Trusty Truth about Leadership
author: Jim Salvucci
summary: Salvucci opens with the silliness of corporate trust falls and uses it to set up his real argument: trust is not produced by a single ceremonial gesture. It is built slowly, is fragile, can evaporate in an instant, and sits at the core of what distinguishes functional leadership from posturing. He anchors the piece on his 4 Cs framework: character and communication generate trust; compromise and collaboration exist only because trust is present. Remove trust, he argues, and compromise and collaboration collapse, taking any real claim to leadership with them. The central metaphor is the basil plant. Watered but otherwise ignored, basil goes leggy, seeds out, and loses its punch. To make a robust plant the gardener has to pinch it back or harvest it properly; use, not just preservation, is what produces vigor. Trust works the same way. Neglect it and it goes to seed. Use it appropriately in daily decisions, compromises, and collaboration, and it grows back bushier than it started. A useful corollary he flags is that trust is situation and context dependent. Trust in one domain does not automatically transfer to another, and changes in circumstance can weaken or even dissolve it. The person who will catch you in a ritual fall may still not have your back in a real crisis. The how-to sections describe character as the accumulated sum of values, experience, temperament, perceptions, image, and behavior, with behavior carrying most of the weight. Communication he treats as message plus audience plus clarity. The illustration is the lout versus the taciturn colleague, and it does the work cleanly: behavior over time is how teams read character, and a consistently reliable presence earns increasingly more trust without ever asking for it. Losing trust he treats as almost embarrassingly easy. Betrayal and failure to follow through are the obvious routes, but neglect is the close second, and undervaluing trust (assuming it will be there through thick and thin) is just another form of neglect. Trust is also inherently transactional, meaning a leader cannot demand trust they are not also extending, and even the appearance of betrayal or indifference is enough to break it.
points: The central argument of this piece is grounded in the author's engagement with how real people think and act, not in idealized or abstract reasoning.
The takeaway is actionable,it can be implemented at the classroom or school level without waiting for policy change or external resources.
The piece challenges a common default assumption in education practice and offers a concrete alternative framed by evidence or lived experience.
The stakes are clear: what happens if leaders or teachers adopt this approach, and what is the cost of continuing the current default.
quotes: Real trust takes a lot more than a momentary exertion of fellowship or a pronounced preference for not seeing another human crack their head on the linoleum. In reality, the mechanics of trust can be complicated and dynamic, which is why the best leaders have a profound appreciation for trust and carefully cultivate and nurture it.

Much like the noggins of your colleagues who recklessly fling themselves backward, hoping you will break their fall, trust is fragile. It can disappear in a flash, delivering a fatal blow to many a relationship or organization.

The first two of the 4 Cs—character and communication—help generate and foster trust. It’s the second two, though—compromise and collaboration—that exist only because of the presence of genuine trust.
If you don’t use it, it just goes to seed, losing all its value. By harvesting trust in relationships, you encourage the growth of more trust. You spurn trust at its peril.

Trust over here doesn’t necessarily translate into trust over there. Just because someone trusts you to catch them in a freefall doesn’t mean they’ll trust you have their back in a crisis or not stab them in it when no one’s looking.

Leaders indicate that they are worthy of trust through their sound character and clear communication. That behavior serves as a model for team members who thereby show that they deserve the leader’s trust.
For me to truly trust you as a leader, you must regularly demonstrate that you truly trust me as a team member. If not, the vital give-and-take aspect of our relationship will crumble.

Trust—no matter how essential to strengthening relationships—is fragile. Even the appearance of betrayal, neglect, or undervaluing can obliterate trust while just a hint of untrustworthiness can ruin a relationship.” Archived from On Leading With Greatness (Substack) on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
